"Thomas, can I tell you something weird?"
"Always, Mridul."
"Today in chemistry, the new teacher asked where I'm from. I said Guwahati. She said, 'No, but where are you really from?'"
"Huh."
"And last week, the shopkeeper said, 'Your Hindi is so good!' I was born here, in Pune. I've spoken Hindi my whole life."
"Did you say anything?"
"No. It's always small. Nobody means anything. But it happens every week."
"Every week?"

When I moved from my small town to a Bengaluru school in Class 9, I heard the same sentence again and again. I'm Rehana. "Your English is so good for a girl from a small town!"
The first time, from a teacher, I said thank you. The second time, from a parent at a meeting, I smiled. By the tenth, I stopped smiling.
My friend Lakshmi once said, "They're complimenting you." And maybe they were. But every compliment came with a surprise attached. As if I shouldn't be able to.
It wasn't one big thing. It was a hundred small things that told me I didn't quite belong.
Now I read aloud in class anyway. Loudly.

qa.q: What sentence did Rehana hear again and again?
qa.a: "Your English is so good for a girl from a small town!"

qa.q: What did Rehana feel by the tenth time?
qa.a: Rehana felt tired and hurt, sensing each compliment carried surprise that Rehana could speak well.

qa.q: What could help someone like Rehana in a new school?
qa.a: Friends and teachers who notice the pattern and stop adding surprise to compliments, and a safe person like Lakshmi to talk it through with.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi seem to see the comments?
qa.a: Lakshmi sees them as compliments, perhaps not noticing the repeated surprise that makes Rehana feel like an outsider.

grounding: Shows a teenager repeatedly told her English is good for a small-town girl, where small remarks add up to feeling she doesn't belong.

Suraj, a scholarship student, came in today. He topped the physics test. He said that since then, classmates keep saying, "Wow, you're surprisingly smart," and one boy, Uday, said, "You're so sharp for someone from your area."

Aadhya came to the class party in a yellow lehenga, and she looked lovely. I said, loudly, "You look so pretty even though you're dark!" I really meant it as praise. I even thought I was being nice.
